<Heading
  as={"h1"}

  children={"Assign an associate to a path"}
>
</Heading>

<MethodEndpoint
  method={"post"}
  path={"/associates/{id}/assignments"}
  context={"endpoint"}
>
  
</MethodEndpoint>



Puts an associate on pathId for a new interval, raising LaborAssigned (first assignment) or LaborReassigned (an assignment was already active). The "exactly one ACTIVE assignment per associate" invariant is enforced by construction, not by rejecting a second call: if the associate already has an active assignment, it is closed first (its hours are logged against the associate's shift) and the new one starts — this matches how rebalancing actually happens on the floor, a supervisor moves someone without first "unassigning" them. The assignment requires the associate hold the path's required certification (by convention, the Certification with the same name as the PathId — e.g. path "pack" requires certification "pack"), and is rejected if the associate is currently on a logged break or their shift has ended. Because each call closes the prior interval and raises an event, a blind retry would double-apply it, so this route is protected by the Idempotency-Key header (ADR-0027): a retried request with the same key and body replays the first response.

Required on every POST: the service runs on Postgres in every deployment (ADR-0038) and rejects a request without it with 400 idempotency-key-required. Reuse the SAME key for retries of one logical request (same body) — the first response, success or business error, is stored and replayed byte-for-byte for the key's TTL (24h by default) — and a NEW key for each new logical request. Reusing a key with a different request (method, path or body) is rejected with 409 idempotency-key-reused. A key that is not 1-128 printable ASCII characters that start and end with a visible character is a 400 idempotency-key-invalid. The pattern describes the header as sent on the wire (ADR-0042): the key itself (1-128 characters, visible first and last character), optionally followed by spaces or tabs. That trailing whitespace is HTTP optional whitespace (RFC 9112 field-line grammar): the HTTP stack drops it before the service reads the value (RFC 9110 section 5.5), so it is never part of the key. Leading whitespace is not in the pattern because HTTP clients do not send it. Every POST of this service takes the key; the key is global (looked up by key alone), so one key must never be reused across routes.","schema":{"type":"string","minLength":1,"pattern":"^[!-~]([ -~]{0,126}[!-~])?[ \\t]*$"},"example":"3f1d6a4e-9c0b-4a39-8f0f-5b2d1c7e9a10"}]}
